evidence.craft: Read experiments/run.py, experiments/figure.py, test_highrecall.py and the dependency chain qual-lowrate/qualrate.py -> qual-labelaudit/qualaudit.py -> qual-gate/qualgate.py and qual-real/qualreal.py. Compact, readable, seeded, stdlib-only, reuses the track's estimator instead of copying it. Nits a reviewer would raise: run.py:32-33 skip branch is dead (draw always returns >= 2 per stratum, so `skipped` is always 0); `import run as real` puts a module named `run` in sys.modules (fragile if another `run` is imported); run.py writes results.txt into the tree with no output flag; the draw silently caps the negative stratum at its size (see defects).
evidence.claims: Every number in the README and project.json traces to results.txt, and the limitations (not an LLM, weak classifier, one corpus, Wald only, no FPC) are stated plainly. But: (a) the table titled '200 audited items' includes x4.0 cells at shares 0.3 and 0.5 that audited 180 and 140 items, because the coder-negative stratum has only 40 items and draw() caps it without reallocating; (b) the headline 'best share each ... 0.119' for the recall-1.00 coder is the share-0 (positives-only) cell, not shown in the README table, whose best shown cell is 0.120; (c) 'the recall 1.00 coder is fine (0.95-0.97)' - at 200 items it is 0.942-0.969, at 100 0.934-0.954; (d) 'yes, a low rate helps' is relative to equal allocation; against proportional allocation (25.9% of the audit for the recall-0.90 coder, analytic width 0.117) the gain of the 10-20% share is about 1.5%, which the README does not say.
evidence.fitness: A researcher can build on it: reproducible byte-for-byte, seeded, small, and it answers the open question left by qual-lowrate. Nearest prior work: Cochran (1977) ch. 5 (stratified variance, Neyman vs proportional allocation, and the known small gain of stratification for proportions unless stratum proportions differ widely), prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al. 2023, cited in qual-lowrate but not here) and the classifier-assisted sampling-for-evaluation literature (e.g. Bennett & Carvalho 2010; Sawade et al. 2010; Katariya et al. 2012), none of which this README cites beyond Cochran. The width results are a closed-form consequence of Cochran's formula (my analytic widths match the Monte Carlo to 0.003); the only empirical content beyond the formula is the coverage failure of Wald intervals when audited negatives are all zero, which is also well known. Sound, not new; a step in a programme rather than a publishable result.
evidence.domain: Stratified estimator, Wald SE and Neyman allocation are textbook-correct (Cochran 5.2-5.5). Departures a survey statistician would flag: no proportional-allocation baseline (the standard comparator, which is never worse than SRS); the coder is binarised at one cut-off when the continuous naive-Bayes score is available for multi-stratum or difference/regression (PPI) estimation, so 'no gain over a random audit' is specific to two strata; the cut-off k = ratio x (number of human positives in the evaluated set) uses the evaluation labels (run.py:53 -> qual-gate/qualgate.py:40); Wald coverage failure with zero-variance strata is acknowledged but the remedy is left open; FPC ignored even where the x4.0 negative stratum is audited in full (40 of 40).

defects.what: Research design: the comparison omits proportional allocation, the standard comparator, and the width results are a closed-form consequence of Cochran's stratified variance (Monte Carlo matches the formula within 0.003); 'yes, a low rate helps' is only relative to equal allocation (gain vs proportional about 1.5%); nearest prior work (prediction-powered inference, classifier-assisted sampling for evaluation) is not cited here

The x4.0 coder's negative stratum has 40 items; qr.draw caps the negative audit at 40 without reallocating the rest, so cells labelled '200 audited items' at shares 0.3/0.5 audited 180/140 items (400-item row: 361/321/241 at 0.2/0.3/0.5); the README table and section-5 mean over coders mix budgets
Tests never execute run.py: one test parses the committed results.txt, the other checks dependency code on a synthetic corpus; 3/3 seeded mutants in run.py survived
Coder cut-off k = ratio x sum(human) uses the evaluation set's human labels, so the 'coder' knows the estimand's numerator; not deployable as written and unstated
Headline '0.119 (best share each)' for the recall-1.00 coder is the share-0 positives-only cell, not in the README table, whose best shown cell is 0.120
'The recall 1.00 coder is fine (0.95-0.97)': results.txt gives 0.942-0.969 at 200 items and 0.934-0.954 at 100
Dead branch: qr.draw always returns >= 2 items per stratum when share > 0, so `skipped` is always 0

verdict: The numbers are right: the experiment reruns byte-identically, and an independent numpy/Cochran recomputation reproduces the prevalence, the baseline, the Neyman shares, the width table (within 0.003 for shares >= 0.1) and the low-share coverage failure. Where it falls short of a survey-statistics referee: the width results follow in closed form from Cochran's stratified variance, the standard proportional-allocation baseline is missing (against it the 'low rate helps' gain is about 1.5%), the x4.0 cells labelled 200 items audited 180 or 140 because the 40-item negative stratum is silently capped, and the tests never run the experiment code (3/3 mutants survive). Honest limitations, a sound and reproducible step in the qual track, not a new result. Does not meet the bar (verification 1, claims 2).
